content: Phototoxicity is a phenomenon observed in live-cell fluorescence microscopy, where the illumination of a fluorescent molecule, specifically its fluorescently active site known as a fluorophore, leads to the selective death of the cells expressing it. Although the exact mechanisms are not fully understood, it is widely accepted that the primary cause of phototoxicity is the generation of oxygen radicals through non-radiative energy transfer. In fluorescence microscopy, photons of a specific wavelength excite the electrons of the fluorophore to higher energy states. When these excited electrons return to a lower energy state, they emit photons with lower energy, resulting in the emission of light at a longer wavelength. This process is referred to as the Stokes shift. However, not all the energy is utilized for this radiative energy transfer. In some cases, the energy is transferred to oxygen molecules, leading to the formation of highly reactive oxygen radicals. These radicals are extremely toxic to living cells and can cause cell death within seconds. The degree of phototoxicity in live cells is highly dependent on the type of fluorescent molecule used. The discovery and development of fluorescent proteins, such as green fluorescent protein (GFP), have provided researchers with fluorochromes that exhibit significantly lower phototoxic effects compared to smaller, chemically synthesized fluorescent molecules like FITC or rhodamine. A phototoxic substance is defined as a chemical compound that becomes toxic only when exposed to light. Examples of such substances include certain medications, such as tetracycline antibiotics and methyl aminolevulinate, as well as some cold-pressed essential oils, like bergamot oil, and plant juices from sources such as parsley and hogweed. The 3T3 Neutral Red Phototoxicity Test (3T3 NRU PT) is an in vitro toxicological assay designed to evaluate the cytotoxic and phototoxic effects of a test substance on murine fibroblasts in the presence or absence of UVA light. The 3T3 NRU PT is capable of identifying substances that are phototoxic in vivo after systemic application and distribution to the skin, as well as compounds that may act as phototoxicants following topical application to the skin. The reliability and relevance of this assay have been validated, demonstrating its predictive value when compared to acute phototoxicity effects observed in vivo in both animals and humans. This assay is a relatively recent development and has been adopted by regulatory agencies such as the OECD and FDA as an accepted method for assessing the phototoxic potential of test substances. Additionally, other testing methods are being developed, including in vitro toxicology models that utilize reconstituted tissues and novel photo-sensitization testing models. These methods aim to evaluate how a compound may react when applied to the skin and subsequently exposed to solar-simulated light.
